Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, i need a prompt for a writer to make a spoken audio guide for the Harborlight Museum’s small exhibition “Signals at the Edge: Working the North Reach.” It’s about people who worked around North Reach harbor from 1910 to 1975, especially fog, signaling, and getting boats safely through. Make it welcoming to a general museum visitor, not only people who know maritime history. The guide should sound natural aloud, with clear sentences and enough pauses in the ideas that a listener can look at an object while listening. Please don’t turn it into a lecture or a dramatic story. It should be informed and vivid, but not sentimental.

The route has six stops, and the writer should create one connected guide of about 750 to 900 spoken words total, divided by stop. Keep this order and use the stop titles as headings. Stop 1, “A harbor in the fog,” is at the entrance map. Stop 2, “The bell and the buoy,” is beside the brass fog bell and the small painted buoy. Stop 3, “Signals across the water,” is at the lamp-and-flag display. Stop 4, “The watch desk,” is the reconstructed harbor office desk with a logbook and weather chart. Stop 5, “A changing harbor,” is the photograph wall about new radios and the decline of some older jobs. Stop 6, “Out toward the breakwater,” is at the large window looking north. The guide should make the movement from one stop to the next understandable, but don’t add a seventh stop or invent objects that aren’t listed here.

Here are the basic facts to work with. North Reach is a fictional harbor on a cold, exposed coast. The entrance channel is narrow and its marker buoy can be hard to see in heavy fog. Before reliable radio sets were installed in harbor vessels, crews relied on shore lights, flags in clear weather, bells, and local knowledge of the channel. The bell in the exhibition was used at the outer station from 1928 to 1959; it was rung by hand when visibility was poor. The painted buoy beside it is a scale model, not the original buoy. The lamp display includes a green harbor lamp, two signal flags, and a hand-cranked lamp used for short messages. Don’t claim a particular flag arrangement means anything unless the prompt’s source notes below say so.

The office desk is a reconstruction based on photographs, not a surviving original desk. Its open logbook is a facsimile. A weather chart on the desk records a thick fog on 14 October 1946 and notes that two boats waited outside the channel until conditions improved. It does not say that either boat was in danger or that the bell alone guided them. The chart also shows wind direction and tide marks, which can be mentioned as details a visitor might notice. The photo wall includes a 1962 picture of radio operator Lena Ortiz at a receiver, a 1937 image of two signal keepers on the outer station steps, and a 1974 view of the harbor entrance after a new radio mast was installed. The mast made communication easier, but don’t say it ended fog or made the harbor risk-free. Older signal-keeping work became less common over time, though the museum material doesn’t give a date when it stopped completely.

Please include these supplied remarks exactly as written, including punctuation. They can be introduced naturally, but don’t edit the wording:
Mara Bell, whose family worked at the outer station: “We thought the fog was a wall, until the bell answered.”
Lena Ortiz, in a recorded interview: “The radio gave us another voice, not a clearer sea.”
A visitor comment recorded in the exhibition book: “I never noticed how much waiting was part of the work.”

Use the following source notes exactly as written wherever relevant, rather than replacing them with a general reference to notes. Object card 17: “Brass fog bell, outer station, 1928–1959. Hand-rung during poor visibility.” Object card 18: “Painted buoy model. Scale model made for the Harborlight Museum display.” Logbook note: “14 October 1946: thick fog at the channel entrance. Two boats held outside until visibility improved.” Photo caption: “Lena Ortiz at the harbor radio receiver, 1962.” These are the exact supplied texts; it’s fine to place them as spoken quotations or to have the guide point out the wording on the display, but keep their words unchanged. The guide should not imply the logbook note gives a rescue story.

At stop 3, explain cautiously that signals depended on visibility and on people knowing how to read them. The notes don’t specify what the two flags mean, so the writer should not assign them a message. At stop 4, connect the weather chart and logbook to observation and waiting, without claiming the desk or logbook are original. At stop 5, use the radio material to show a change in communication, not a simple story of technology replacing all older skills. At stop 6, bring the listener back to the view north and the narrow channel, and let the ending be reflective but not a conclusion about the whole history of the harbor.

There is one access detail that matters for directions. The normal route from stop 4 to stop 5 passes the east lift. If the east lift is unavailable on the visit date, the guide’s direction at stop 4 must offer the west gallery route instead and say that staff can point it out. Don’t state that the lift is currently working or unavailable, and don’t promise anything about lift operation. Keep the alternate direction conditional, and don’t let that route change the order or content of the six stops.

Please write for listening rather than silent reading. Avoid long strings of dates, unexplained specialist terms, invented dialogue, and claims about what a named person felt unless those feelings are stated in the remarks above. You can explain “outer station” briefly as the harbor post near the channel entrance. Don’t add visitor instructions beyond looking, listening, or following the route directions noted here. The guide should distinguish the real bell and the model buoy, as well as the reconstructed desk and facsimile logbook. Make the six sections feel connected without repeating the same background facts at every stop.

For the ending, use the north-facing window as the final point of attention, and leave room for listeners to look at the water. Please don’t invent a final event, claim the channel is safe now, or add a recommendation to the museum. The last section should still include meaningful information about the view, the entrance channel, or the changing ways people watched it; it shouldn’t end with a generic thank-you. Keep all six stops and the access condition in the finished guide prompt, and make sure the three remarks and four source-note texts remain exactly as supplied.", "output": "Write a spoken audio guide for the Harborlight Museum’s small exhibition **“Signals at the Edge: Working the North Reach.”** The exhibition covers people who worked around North Reach harbor from 1910 to 1975, especially fog, signaling, and helping boats pass safely through. Address general museum visitors, including people unfamiliar with maritime history. Use natural spoken language, clear sentences, and ideas with enough breathing room for listeners to look at the objects. Keep the tone informed and vivid, not lecture-like, dramatic, or sentimental.

## Length and route

Create one connected guide of about 750–900 spoken words, divided into six stops. Use these titles as headings and keep them in this order:

1. **A harbor in the fog** — entrance map.
2. **The bell and the buoy** — brass fog bell and small painted buoy.
3. **Signals across the water** — lamp-and-flag display.
4. **The watch desk** — reconstructed harbor office desk, logbook, and weather chart.
5. **A changing harbor** — photographs about new radios and the decline of some older jobs.
6. **Out toward the breakwater** — large window looking north.

Make the movement between stops understandable. Do not add another stop or invent objects beyond those listed.

## Historical information and objects

North Reach is a fictional harbor on a cold, exposed coast. Its entrance channel is narrow, and its marker buoy can be hard to see in heavy fog. Before reliable radio sets were installed in harbor vessels, crews relied on shore lights, flags in clear weather, bells, and local knowledge of the channel.

The brass fog bell was used at the outer station from 1928 to 1959 and was rung by hand when visibility was poor. The painted buoy beside it is a scale model, not the original. The lamp display includes a green harbor lamp, two signal flags, and a hand-cranked lamp used for short messages. Do not assign meanings to a flag arrangement unless the supplied notes below do so.

The watch desk is a reconstruction based on photographs, not a surviving original. Its open logbook is a facsimile. A weather chart records thick fog on 14 October 1946 and notes that two boats waited outside the channel until conditions improved. It does not say that either boat was in danger or that the bell alone guided them. The chart also shows wind direction and tide marks, which visitors may notice.

The photo wall includes a 1937 image of two signal keepers on the outer station steps, a 1962 picture of radio operator Lena Ortiz at a receiver, and a 1974 view of the harbor entrance after a new radio mast was installed. The mast made communication easier, but do not say it ended fog or made the harbor risk-free. Older signal-keeping work became less common over time; the museum material gives no date when it stopped completely.

## Supplied remarks and display texts

Include these remarks exactly as written, including punctuation. Introduce them naturally, without changing their wording:

Mara Bell, whose family worked at the outer station: “We thought the fog was a wall, until the bell answered.”

Lena Ortiz, in a recorded interview: “The radio gave us another voice, not a clearer sea.”

A visitor comment recorded in the exhibition book: “I never noticed how much waiting was part of the work.”

Use the following source notes exactly as written wherever relevant. They may be spoken as quotations or introduced as wording on the display. Do not replace them with a general reference to notes, and do not imply that the logbook describes a rescue:

Object card 17: “Brass fog bell, outer station, 1928–1959. Hand-rung during poor visibility.”

Object card 18: “Painted buoy model. Scale model made for the Harborlight Museum display.”

Logbook note: “14 October 1946: thick fog at the channel entrance. Two boats held outside until visibility improved.”

Photo caption: “Lena Ortiz at the harbor radio receiver, 1962.”

## Focus for each stop

At stop 3, explain cautiously that signals depended on visibility and on people knowing how to read them. The notes do not specify what the two flags mean, so do not assign them a message. At stop 4, connect the weather chart and logbook to observation and waiting, without describing the desk or logbook as original. At stop 5, present radio as a change in communication, not as a simple replacement of all older skills. At stop 6, return attention to the view north and the narrow channel. Let the ending be reflective without presenting it as a conclusion about the harbor’s entire history.

## Route access

The normal route from stop 4 to stop 5 passes the east lift. If the east lift is unavailable on the visit date, the direction at stop 4 must offer the west gallery route instead and say staff can point it out. Keep this alternative conditional. Do not state that the lift is currently working or unavailable, promise anything about its operation, or let the alternate route change the order or content of the six stops.

## Style and final section

Write for listening rather than silent reading. Avoid long strings of dates, unexplained specialist terms, invented dialogue, and claims about what a named person felt unless that feeling is stated in the supplied remarks. You may briefly explain “outer station” as the harbor post near the channel entrance. Do not add visitor instructions beyond looking, listening, or following the route directions specified here. Clearly distinguish the real bell from the model buoy, and the reconstructed desk from the facsimile logbook. Connect the sections without repeating the same background facts at every stop.

End at the north-facing window, leaving room for listeners to look at the water. The final section must include meaningful information about the view, the entrance channel, or the changing ways people watched it. Do not invent a final event, claim the channel is safe now, add a museum recommendation, or end with a generic thank-you. Include all six stops and the access condition in the guide, and keep all three remarks and all four source-note texts exactly as supplied."}]
